description: Wildlife Sanctuaries and Biosphere Reserves are established in India for the conservation of biodiversity. These protected areas play a crucial role in safeguarding endangered species and delicate ecosystems from human exploitation.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.description: Fundamental definitions and differences between various types of protected areas.

key_concepts.explanation: A natural area where wildlife is conserved in its natural habitat without significant human interference. Limited human activities (like collecting dry wood or minor forest produce) may be permitted by authorities.
A protected area with stricter regulations compared to a sanctuary. No human activities like livestock grazing, hunting, or commercial forestry are allowed inside its boundaries.

A large protected landscape where wildlife, plants, and the traditional lifestyle of local tribals are conserved together. It is divided into three zones: Core (no human activity), Buffer (limited activity), and Transition (human settlements allowed).

sections.title: Historical Conservation Milestones
sections.description: Significant legislative and organizational steps taken globally and in India to protect wildlife.

historical_events.significance: Launched by UNESCO to improve the relationship between humans and the environment and to establish a global network of Biosphere Reserves.
Enacted by the Government of India to protect wildlife, strictly prohibit poaching, and regulate the illegal trade of flora and fauna.
Launched from Jim Corbett National Park to protect the Bengal Tiger from extinction and preserve its natural habitats.
Launched as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme to protect wild elephants, secure their natural habitats, and preserve their migration corridors.

sections.title: Important Biosphere Reserves
sections.description: Major Biosphere Reserves of India and their unique geographical and ecological characteristics.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: Established in 1986, it is India's first Biosphere Reserve. It is highly famous for the Nilgiri Tahr and the Lion-tailed Macaque.
India's first marine biosphere reserve, renowned for its rich coral reefs and the conservation of the Dugong (Sea Cow).
The largest contiguous mangrove forest area in the world and the only natural mangrove habitat of the Royal Bengal Tiger.
A high-altitude biosphere reserve that serves as a crucial habitat for rare species like the Snow Leopard and Himalayan Musk Deer.

key_associations.extra_info: Located in Gujarat, it is the last and only natural habitat of Asiatic Lions in the world.

sections.title: Important Facts and Superlatives
sections.description: Crucial one-liner facts and data points regarding wildlife conservation in India.

important_facts.fact: India's first National Park is 'Jim Corbett National Park', which was originally established in 1936 as Hailey National Park.
There are currently 18 recognized Biosphere Reserves in India, out of which 12 are included in the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR).
The Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is the largest Biosphere Reserve in India in terms of total geographical area.
Dibru-Saikhowa, located in Assam, holds the record for being the smallest Biosphere Reserve in India.
India's largest wildlife sanctuary is the 'Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary' in Gujarat, which is famous for the endangered Indian Wild Ass.
